proposals.impact: reduce zero-start drop-off on quiz intro screen
proposals.observation: In the last 48 hours, 2 sessions hit the quiz intro screen and 0 started the quiz. The furthest-step distribution shows both users stalled at intro_load. That means the intro screen itself is the exit point. Both sessions came via direct traffic, so these are warm visitors who already knew where they were going. They arrived, read the intro, and left without pressing start. The copy or the ask on that screen is not earning the click.
proposals.proposal: Rewrite the quiz intro body copy to reduce the cognitive cost of starting. The current text (see CURRENT_TEXT) frames the quiz as a diagnostic tool, which can feel clinical or high-stakes to someone who already feels anxious about money. The replacement grounds the ask in a single, low-threat sentence that describes what the person will get in concrete terms, then names the time cost exactly. No promises of transformation. No imperative verbs that push. The CTA button label changes from "Start the quiz" to "See my result" because outcome framing converts better than process framing for this ICP.
proposals.current_text:
This short quiz will help you identify your money personality type and understand the behavioural patterns that may be shaping your financial decisions.

It takes around 5 minutes.
proposals.new_text:
Four questions. You'll get a named pattern at the end, with a plain explanation of what it tends to produce in real spending and saving decisions.

It takes three minutes, sometimes less.

proposals.impact: lift Money Vigilance open rate from 66% by testing a more specific subject line
proposals.observation: The Money Vigilance automation has a 66.67% open rate on 12 sends, the highest of the three active automations and well above the Money Avoidance sequence (52.63%) and Money Worship (37.5%). The sequence is working. The opportunity is in the subject line of email 1: if the current subject line is already pulling 66%, a more specific, pattern-named subject line could push that further and set a benchmark for rewriting the weaker automations. Small subject-line edits are low-risk, single-field changes.
proposals.proposal: Replace the email-1 subject line in the Money Vigilance automation with a line that names the specific, lived cost of vigilance rather than the trait itself. Vigilance sounds neutral or even positive to people who have it, so a subject line that reflects the felt experience (the checking, the not-spending even when it would be fine, the guilt after a normal purchase) will create faster recognition. The current subject line is a label. The new one is a mirror.

proposals.impact: restore automated blog publishing and refill the near-empty content queue
proposals.observation: Two GitHub workflow runs failed in the last 24 hours: Daily Blog Post (06:56 UTC) and Funnel-Hack Digest (11:30 UTC). The content queue shows 1 post queued and 47 published. With automated publishing broken, that single queued post will not go out on schedule, the queue will hit zero, and the blog goes dark until the workflow is fixed manually. The blocked-paths rule correctly prevents Fred from editing the workflow file directly, so this proposal targets the most likely cause of the failure: a malformed or stale frontmatter field in the queued post that the workflow's validation step is rejecting.
proposals.proposal: Inspect and correct the frontmatter of the single queued post. Workflow failures on content-publishing pipelines most often trace to a missing required field, a date format mismatch, or a draft flag left as true. Open the queued file, confirm all required frontmatter fields are present and correctly typed (pubDate as YYYY-MM-DD string, draft: false, title non-empty), and save. If the workflow re-runs and passes, that also clears the Funnel-Hack Digest failure because both workflows share the same content source. This is a one-file fix with no structural changes.
